steps.body: To mark thirds on a number line, cut the distance from 0 to 1 into three equal jumps — not three tick marks, three JUMPS.
steps.narration: To mark thirds on a number line, cut the distance from 0 to 1 into three equal jumps — not three tick marks, three JUMPS.

widget.prompt: Place 2/3 on a THIRDS line: count equal jumps from 0.

commonPlacements.feedback: 1/3 is one jump from zero, and the question asked for two of them.

widget.successFeedback: 2/3 — two of the three equal jumps from zero.
widget.lowFeedback: Jumps run FORWARD from 0, so a landing behind the target is short of it — count the jumps again.
widget.highFeedback: That went past 2/3 — the whole trip is three jumps, and only two were asked for.

predict.prompt: Cutting 0 to 1 into thirds, how many JUMPS are there?
predict.reveal: Four marks bound three spaces. Fractions are named by the spaces you travel, not the posts you pass.

cml.actionGoal: Cut, count, and compare equal pieces to see what g3f thirds line really names.
invariants: A fraction names equal shares of ONE whole: the denominator says how many equal pieces the whole became, and the numerator counts them, which is what makes g3f thirds line comparable at all.
misconceptions: Calling unequal pieces fractions, reading the denominator as a count, or comparing fractions that came from different-sized wholes.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the whole changed size, which of these comparisons would stop being trustworthy?

widget.prompt: A garden bed is split into thirds. How many equal pieces are there?

commonErrors.feedback: One is the whole, not the number of pieces — thirds names how many equal parts the whole becomes.
Two equal parts are halves. Thirds cut the same whole into one more piece.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Name the equal pieces the whole was cut into, then count how many of them the question is about.

widget.prompt: Compute 5 × 1/8 as ?/8. What is the numerator?

commonErrors.feedback: 8 is the DENOMINATOR — it names the piece size and never changes when you collect pieces.
Adding the two numbers mixes a count of pieces with a piece size; only the count grows.
